title: Archaeology in India: history, methods, sites and careers
seo_title: Archaeology in India: History, Major Sites and Careers
meta_description: Archaeology in India explained: how it began with the Asiatic Society and the ASI, the methods used today, the major sites and how to build a career in it.
summary: Archaeology in India began in the late 18th century with the Asiatic Society in Calcutta, became an organised state effort when the Archaeological Survey of India was founded in 1861 under Alexander Cunningham, and grew into a scientific discipline under John Marshall, Mortimer Wheeler and Indian archaeologists after 1947. Today universities, the ASI and state departments excavate, date and protect sites from the Stone Age to the colonial period.

paras: Archaeology is the study of the human past through material remains: tools, pottery, buildings, bones, seeds, coins, inscriptions and the soil layers that hold them. Our explainer on [what archaeology is](what-is-archaeology.html) covers the basics. In India it has a particular job. Written records reach back only to Ashoka's inscriptions in the 3rd century BCE, and many later texts are religious, courtly or hard to date. Archaeology is the main source for everything before that, and an essential check on everything after.

It also reaches people the texts ignore: farmers, potters, labourers, women and children, forest and hill communities. The [difference between archaeology and history](difference-between-archaeology-and-history.html) is less about subject than about evidence, and the best work in India now combines both.

sections.h2: The beginnings: the Asiatic Society and antiquarians
paras: Systematic interest in India's past began with the Asiatic Society, founded in Calcutta (now Kolkata) in 1784 by William Jones. Jones is remembered for pointing out the relationship between Sanskrit, Greek and Latin. Members of the Society collected coins, copied inscriptions and described monuments, mostly as part of a colonial project to understand and govern India.

The breakthrough came in 1837, when James Prinsep, secretary of the Society, deciphered the Brahmi script using short donor inscriptions from Sanchi. Within months he could read Ashoka's edicts. This single step opened the inscriptions of early India and made it possible to link texts, coins and monuments. Our explainer on [epigraphy](what-is-epigraphy.html) shows how inscriptions are read today.

sections.h2: Alexander Cunningham and the founding of the ASI
paras: Alexander Cunningham, an army engineer, was the first to survey India's monuments on a large scale. Guided by the travel accounts of the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang, he identified many Buddhist sites, including Sarnath, Sankisa and Shravasti, and explored Sanchi and Bharhut.

In 1861 the colonial government created the post of Archaeological Surveyor with Cunningham at its head. This was the start of the [Archaeological Survey of India](archaeological-survey-of-india.html). Cunningham's tours produced volumes of reports, and he also visited Harappa, collecting a seal he could not explain. The ASI went through periods of closure and revival in its early decades before becoming a permanent department.

sections.h2: John Marshall and the discovery of the Indus cities
paras: Lord Curzon, Viceroy from 1899, revived the ASI and appointed John Marshall as Director General in 1902. The Ancient Monuments Preservation Act of 1904 gave the state legal power to protect sites. Marshall's ASI conserved monuments across India and excavated at Taxila, Sanchi and other sites.

Its most famous result came from work in the early 1920s at Harappa, led by Daya Ram Sahni, and at Mohenjo-daro, led by R. D. Banerji. In 1924 Marshall announced that these finds belonged to a previously unknown Bronze Age civilisation, now called the [Indus Valley Civilization](indus-valley-civilization.html). Indian history was pushed back by some two thousand years almost overnight.

Mortimer Wheeler became Director General in 1944. He introduced stratigraphic excavation using the grid method, insisted on careful recording of layers and trained a generation of Indian archaeologists at field schools, most famously at Taxila. His excavations at Arikamedu near Puducherry linked Roman pottery with Indian layers and gave firm dates to south Indian sequences.

Wheeler's interpretations, especially his suggestion that the Indus cities were destroyed by Aryan invaders, have not stood up to later evidence. But his methods changed Indian archaeology. Our explainer on [how an excavation works](how-an-excavation-works.html) shows what stratigraphic digging means in practice.

Partition left Harappa and Mohenjo-daro in Pakistan. Indian archaeologists set out to find Harappan sites within India and found many: Lothal and Dholavira in Gujarat, Kalibangan in Rajasthan, and Rakhigarhi and Banawali in Haryana. B. B. Lal, H. D. Sankalia, A. Ghosh, R. S. Bisht and others led major projects.

Sankalia, at Deccan College in Pune, built Indian prehistory into a field of its own. Universities at Pune, Baroda, Allahabad (now Prayagraj), Varanasi and elsewhere developed departments of archaeology. Excavations since then have mapped the Neolithic and Chalcolithic cultures of the Deccan and Ganga plains, the early historic cities, and the archaeology of the south, including Adichanallur, Keeladi and Pattanam.

Some excavations have been tied to political debates, most famously at Ayodhya. Archaeology works best when its methods and records are open to scrutiny, and our talk on [excavation headlines](excavation-headlines-evidence-or-exaggeration.html) looks at how to read claims about new finds carefully.

sections.h2: Methods used in Indian archaeology today
paras: Modern Indian archaeology uses the same toolkit as anywhere else, adapted to local conditions.
list: Survey: walking fields, mapping surface finds, and using satellite images, drones and [remote sensing](remote-sensing-in-archaeology-and-heritage-management.html) to find sites.
Excavation: digging by layers, recording every find in its context, and drawing sections and plans.
Dating: radiocarbon, optically stimulated luminescence, pottery sequences, coins and inscriptions. See [how archaeologists date artifacts](how-archaeologists-date-artifacts.html).
Science: archaeobotany (plant remains), zooarchaeology (animal bones), bioarchaeology (human remains), isotope studies and ancient DNA.
Specialist study: pottery, stone tools, beads, metals, [coins](what-is-numismatics.html) and inscriptions.
Documentation and conservation: measured drawing, photography, 3D scanning and protecting what is exposed.

paras: India has thousands of excavated sites. A short list of the most important gives a sense of range. Our [famous archaeological sites in India](famous-archaeological-sites-in-india.html) explainer has more, and the [best archaeology museums in India](best-archaeology-museums-in-india.html) shows where the finds are displayed.

paras: The best way to understand archaeology is to see it in action. A [mock excavation](mock-trench-a-practice-excavation.html) lets students dig, record and interpret a prepared trench in a single session, and our [Prehistory field school](prehistory-field-workshop.html) takes older students into the field. Workshops on [pottery](clay-and-the-past-a-pottery-workshop.html) and [stone tools](stone-tools-up-close.html) show how archaeologists read objects.

Sites near Delhi are good places to start. [Mehrauli Archaeological Park](mehrauli-archaeological-park.html) has layers from the Tomar Rajputs to the British, and Rakhigarhi in Haryana shows a Harappan city under a living village.

Excavation in India needs a licence. Under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act of 1958 and its rules, the ASI grants permission for excavation and exploration, including to universities and state departments, through its Central Advisory Board of Archaeology. Each licence holder must report on the work, and the ASI's annual review, Indian Archaeology: A Review, has summarised fieldwork across the country for decades.

Antiquities are also controlled. The Antiquities and Art Treasures Act of 1972 requires registration of certain antiquities and bans their export without a licence. Chance finds of treasure fall under the Indian Treasure Trove Act of 1878. These rules exist because looting and the illegal art trade have taken thousands of sculptures and objects out of India, some of which have been returned in recent years.

sections.h2: New directions: science, communities and the recent past
paras: Indian archaeology has changed a great deal since 2000. Scientific dating is more widely available, and studies of plant remains, animal bones, isotopes and ancient DNA now shape debates about farming, diet, migration and climate. Landscape archaeology looks at whole regions rather than single mounds, and underwater archaeology has explored submerged sites off Gujarat and Tamil Nadu.

There is also more attention to people who were long left out: women, children, labourers, nomadic and forest communities. Our talk on [gender and everyday life in archaeology](gender-and-everyday-life-in-archaeology.html) explores this. Community archaeology involves people who live near sites in research and protection, and historical archaeology studies forts, cemeteries, plantations and factories of the last few centuries.

Most archaeologists in India work for the ASI, state archaeology departments, universities, museums or research institutes. Others work in heritage management, conservation, cultural resource management for infrastructure projects, tourism, publishing and digital heritage. Salaries in government posts follow pay commissions; private and project work varies.

The usual path is a bachelor's degree in history, anthropology or a science, followed by an MA in archaeology or ancient Indian history and archaeology, and then a PhD for research and teaching. The ASI's Institute of Archaeology (Pandit Deendayal Upadhyaya Institute of Archaeology) in Greater Noida runs a two-year postgraduate diploma. Our guides on [archaeology courses in India](archaeology-courses-in-india.html) and [how to become an archaeologist in India](how-to-become-an-archaeologist-in-india.html) list institutions and exams.

Talaash Heritage runs career sessions such as [archaeology after Class 12](archaeology-after-class-12.html) and [BA to MA archaeology pathways](ba-ma-archaeology-pathways.html) for students and parents.

faq.q: Who is the father of Indian archaeology?
faq.a: Alexander Cunningham is usually called the father of Indian archaeology. He surveyed hundreds of sites and became the first head of the Archaeological Survey of India in 1861. Some writers give the title to William Jones, who founded the Asiatic Society in 1784.

faq.q: When was the Archaeological Survey of India founded?
faq.a: The ASI was founded in 1861, with Alexander Cunningham as Archaeological Surveyor. It was revived and strengthened under Lord Curzon and John Marshall in the early 1900s, and today works under the Ministry of Culture.

faq.q: Who discovered the Indus Valley Civilization?
faq.a: Daya Ram Sahni excavated at Harappa in 1921 and R. D. Banerji at Mohenjo-daro in 1922. John Marshall, Director General of the ASI, announced the discovery of a new civilisation in 1924. Earlier visitors such as Charles Masson and Cunningham had seen Harappa without recognising its age.

faq.q: What methods do archaeologists use in India?
faq.a: Survey on foot and with satellite images and drones, stratigraphic excavation, dating by radiocarbon, luminescence, pottery, coins and inscriptions, and scientific study of plants, animal bones, human remains and ancient DNA. Recording and conservation are part of every project.

faq.q: Which is the largest archaeological site in India?
faq.a: Rakhigarhi in Haryana is often described as the largest Harappan site in India, with several mounds spread over a large area. Hampi in Karnataka is one of the largest historic city sites.

faq.q: How can I become an archaeologist in India?
faq.a: Take a bachelor's degree in history, anthropology or a related subject, then an MA in archaeology or ancient Indian history and archaeology. Field training and a PhD open research and teaching posts. ASI and state jobs are filled through recruitment notices and exams.

faq.q: Can school students take part in an excavation?
faq.a: Real excavations are licensed and usually limited to trained staff and university students. School students can learn the method through mock excavations, museum workshops and supervised field schools designed for their age.

posts.hook: One man read a forgotten script in 1837 and opened up a thousand years of history.
posts.caption: James Prinsep cracked Brahmi using short donor inscriptions at Sanchi. Within months he was reading Ashoka's edicts for the first time in centuries.

posts.hook: At any excavated site, look at the trench walls.
posts.caption: The layered soil in a section is the archaeologist's calendar. Lower is usually older. Changes in colour or texture can mean a new floor, a fire or a flood.
Our mock excavation recreates a trench with layers and finds. Students dig, record and interpret, just as archaeologists do. Available for schools and colleges on request.
